findings.source_quote: κἀκεῖ δακρύοντας ἡμᾶς λιμῷ φόβῳ τε καὶ πληγαῖς, ὅπως μή τι προπετὲς λαλήσωμεν τῶν αὐτοῖς μὴ δοκούντων, ἔτι δὲ καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα ἡμῶν ἀλλάξαντες, πωλῆσαι ἠδυνήθησαν.
findings.english_quote: There, by hunger, fear, and blows, though we were weeping, they managed to sell us, after also changing our names so that we would not rashly say anything they did not want said.
findings.issue: The draft changes the attachments within the coercion sequence. λιμῷ φόβῳ τε καὶ πληγαῖς explains the children's weeping, but the English makes hunger, fear, and blows the means by which the men managed the sale. It also relocates the purpose of preventing unwanted speech to the name change, whereas the Greek places that purpose with the preceding coercive treatment and then introduces the additional renaming.
findings.suggested_revision: Recast the sequence, for example: “There, with us weeping from hunger, fear, and blows—all to keep us from rashly saying anything they did not want said—and after also changing our names, they managed to sell us.” Review the revised attachments afresh.

findings.source_quote: οὗ φανέντος ἐν βασιλείᾳ τῶν θεοσεβησάντων ὁ ... ων ἀθανάτως καὶ ἀλύπως βιῶσαι ἔχει
findings.english_quote: There is an account about a certain man: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain.
findings.issue: The main text defensibly attaches τῶν θεοσεβησάντων to the incomplete subject represented by ὁ ... ων. However, the notes discuss the sense of βασιλείᾳ without disclosing the material alternative attachment of the genitive to βασιλείᾳ: “in the kingdom/kingship of those who have revered God.” The three-dot gap and surviving fragments are faithfully represented; the gap itself is not a coverage failure or a reason to require restoration.
findings.suggested_revision: Add a source-quoted note identifying both possible attachments of τῶν θεοσεβησάντων and explaining why the main text associates it with the incomplete subject. Distinguish that syntactic choice from recovery of missing wording. Retain the exact three-dot gap and the existing disclosure that no restoration has been supplied.

findings.source_quote: ἀφ’ ἧς τὰ ἐμαυτῆς. ἀπέλαβον τέκνα
findings.english_quote: from the time I have recovered my own children
findings.issue: The English gives a defensible continuous construction, but silently passes over the supplied edition's full stop after ἐμαυτῆς, which interrupts that construction. This is an image-checked printed punctuation feature, not evidence of an OCR error or missing wording.
findings.suggested_revision: Add a source_issues note quoting “ἀφ’ ἧς τὰ ἐμαυτῆς. ἀπέλαβον τέκνα”. Explain that the English reads the surviving words continuously despite the printed stop, without changing the supplied Greek or restoring any text. Classify this as a disclosed editorial punctuation feature, not a publication-blocking source corruption.

findings.source_quote: ἐγὼ μόνος ἄσπλαγχνός εἰμι ὅτι μὴ βούλομαι ὑμᾶς συνεστιασθῆναι τῇ μητρί, βαπτίσας αὐτὴν σήμερον;
findings.english_quote: Am I alone unfeeling, because I do not want you to dine with your mother by baptizing her today?
findings.issue: The placement of “by baptizing her today” leaves its agent unclear and readily attaches it to “you”. The Greek nominative singular βαπτίσας refers to Peter, not to the children. This ambiguity is introduced by the English rather than inherited from the Greek.
findings.suggested_revision: Make Peter the explicit baptizer, for example: “Am I alone unfeeling, because I do not want you to dine with your mother after I have baptized her today?” Submit the revised sentence for fresh review.

findings.source_quote: Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔστιν τοῦτο νηστεία βαπτίσματος, ἢ μὴ δι’ αὐτὸ γέγονεν.
findings.english_quote: But this is not a baptismal fast, since it did not take place for that purpose.
findings.issue: An explanatory connection between the clauses is contextually defensible, so “since” need not be rejected merely because the construction is unusual. Nevertheless, the note does not preserve an English alternative retaining the printed disjunctive ἤ. Its “unless it took place for that purpose” expresses a conditional criterion but is not transparently a rendering of the supplied ἢ μὴ clause. The distinction between direct rendering and contextual paraphrase needs disclosure; print verification is not the missing evidence.
findings.suggested_revision: Explicitly compare the causal main text with a source-transparent explanatory disjunction such as “But this is not a baptismal fast—or, rather, it did not take place for that purpose.” If “since” is retained, explain why the printed “or” is construed explanatorily and preserve the disjunctive alternative in the note. Label the “unless” formulation as a contextual paraphrase rather than an alternative supplied Greek reading. Any revised main text requires fresh review.
